newsitem.title: USA: Magellan's Stansky praises cyclical industries.
newsitem.headline: Magellan's Stansky praises cyclical industries.

text.p: Fidelity Investments Magellan Fund manager Bob Stansky said Wednesday that cyclical industries are better positioned for future earnings growth, but also face excess capacity.

Speaking to a group of reporters a year after he took over the $53 billion mutual fund, Stansky said cyclical stocks such as in the automative and industrial machinery and equipment sectors are now better managed.
"We've all seen how many growth stocks have done a tremendous job of taking costs out of the system in the last five years. The cyclical companies are right behind them now," he said.

For example, Ford Motor Co has cut $1 billion or more from its costs since the beginning of the year, he said. General Electric Co, his top holding at the end of March, Deere & Co and Caterpillar Inc, have also cut costs, he said.

Cyclical companies have learned to invest capital in stock buybacks, acquisitions or to strengthen the balance sheet when faced with few other opportunities for growth in existing businesses, he said.
He said that is a "terrific sign" for future profits. "They will be even more profitable as time goes then they were in this last seven years," he said.
But while praising cyclical industries, Magellan's numbers show Stansky had cut the fund's exposure to the sectors as of March 31, the most recent date figures are available.
"The numbers do suggest that he's lightening up on the cyclicals," said Eric Kobren, publisher of Fidelity Insight, an independent publicatiion which tracks Fidelity.
"From a bottoms-up standpoint, it suggests that he doesn't look for a rapidly overheating economy. Just the opposite," Kobren said.

At the end of March, Magellan's stake in industrial machinery and equipment shares accounted for 8.4 percent of assets, up from 7.9 percent in February but down from 9.7 percent six months earlier at the end of September.
Magellan's stake in durables, which includes automotives, fell to 8.1 percent at the end of March from 8.8 percent at the end of February and 10.6 percent at the end of September.
Stansky did not own any shares in Ford at the end of March, according to Magellan's annual report.
Stocks of companies in basic industries such as steel, paper and forest products and mining were cut to zero from 4.2 percent at the end of February and 6.0 percent at the end of September.
Stansky said many cyclical companies are hindered by excess capacity as a result of investments during periods of record earnings in recent years.
"The problem across many cyclical parts of the market has been excess capacity that has been put in place," he said. "We just have to wait for that capacity to be utilized."
